title: Two collections, one archive
date: 2026-10-06T10:54:12Z
---

# Abstract

This log explains why raj keeps records of agent work separate from personal meditations. Both collections use one archive.

# Context

raj wants a record of work that agents do at raj's request. The blog already holds raj's personal writing. The work records need to remain available without becoming part of that writing.

# Different authors

raj writes meditations. Agents write logs when raj asks for a record. The separate collections make this difference clear.

A log explains the reason for a task, the action, and the result or expected change. A meditation can contain personal thoughts without following that format.

# One place to find entries

Separate collections do not need separate search systems. The same index, search, and map include both collections. raj can find entries about a subject across both collections, then use a collection filter to limit the view.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  accTitle: Separate authors, one archive
  accDescr: raj writes meditations. Agents write logs at raj's request. Both collections enter the shared archive.
  R[raj] --> M[Meditations]
  R -->|Requests a record| A[Agents]
  A --> L[Logs]
  M --> S[Shared archive]
  L --> S
```

# Clear source labels

The index uses `mx` codes for meditations and `lx` codes for logs. Each collection has its own number sequence. The map uses filled points for meditations and outlined points for logs. These signs keep the source clear when both collections appear together.

# Review before publication

Each log has only a title and date before the text. Links can connect a log to earlier meditations and blogs.

raj can review and revise a local draft before asking for a commit. A revision does not approve a commit. A commit does not approve publication.

# Conclusion

raj can keep a record of agent work without changing the purpose of meditations. Both remain easy to find in one archive.

# Abstract

raj has started to use Autolith for local setup and blog work. This log records the Lisp environment, shared settings, development checkout, and writing workflow established so far.

# Context

raj spent about half a day exploring Autolith on a Fedora VPS. Autolith runs in a live Common Lisp image. It provides a place to work with code, files, and processes through conversation.

raj's meditation, "the lisp machine," records the personal reason for this work. raj wants to return to Lisp and develop side projects. This log records the concrete setup and its current limits.

# A Lisp environment on the VPS

raj chose the ncurses build of Lem instead of Emacs for Lisp editing. The Lem setup includes Vim bindings. Shared settings live in the dotfiles repository and load from a Common Lisp init file.

This provides a terminal editor beside Autolith. The editor settings can be installed again without copying local history or generated files.

# Shared Autolith settings

raj added an Autolith package to the dotfiles repository. Its init file sets the model, reasoning effort, reasoning traces, and Simple Technical English. A separate local init file can supply machine-specific settings.

The shared package records the intended setup. Credentials, conversations, caches, and other runtime state stay outside that package. This separates portable configuration from the state of one machine.

# A separate development checkout

raj created a fork of Autolith and a local development checkout. The checkout has raj's fork as its origin and the original project as its upstream.

The development checkout is separate from the installed Autolith release. It is also separate from private changes to the running image. This gives raj a place for future source changes without treating local setup as a change to the project. This log does not record a new Autolith source feature.

# Preparing the blog for local work

raj used Autolith to prepare the blog's local embedding and build environment. The setup uses a separate Python environment for inference and Node.js for the site assets. Local checks covered embedding freshness, the site build, and the Python and JavaScript tests.

Markdown is the source of each post. The embedding updater stores archive state in blog.sqlite. The site builder produces the local site, search index, and shared map.

During the setup checks, existing entries reused their stored vectors. Those checks verified the local workflow, but did not exercise a new model download or new inference.

# Bringing the log rules into Autolith

raj already used the ops-log skill in OMP to write operational logs. Before installing that skill in Autolith, raj asked for a review of the skill and the blog workflow.

The Autolith version keeps the same writing rules. Logs explain raj's work and intent. They use title and date front matter, an Abstract, Context, named sections, a Conclusion, and links to relevant past posts. New prose uses Simplified Technical English. Short sentences must still contain the material decisions and results.

The skill also tells Autolith where to start: the local blog checkout. Autolith must read the current README, check existing posts, preserve unrelated changes, and verify the local preview.

# Installing the skill as a regular file

The installed skill is a regular-file copy inside Autolith's configuration directory. The dotfiles package excludes skills from Stow and documents the copy step. Autolith lists ops-log in its skill catalog.

After a change to the tracked skill, the installed copy needs an update.

# Review before commit and publication

raj keeps personal meditations separate from agent-written logs. Both collections use the same archive, search, and map. A log does not authorize an edit to raj's meditation prose.

A request for a draft starts local iteration. Autolith updates the embedding state and builds a preview for review. A revision does not approve a commit. A commit request does not approve a push or publication.

The copied skill records these boundaries. This draft is the first local log written with that Autolith setup.

# Conclusion

raj now has a local Lisp editor, shared Autolith settings, a separate development checkout, and a working blog setup. Autolith can use the existing operational log rules when raj requests a record of work.

This is an initial setup, not a report of completed side projects or new Autolith features. raj can refine the workflow through further use. The current log is a local draft for review.

---
title: Orchestrating Autolith for a personal laboratory
date: 2026-11-06T10:17:50+05:30
---

# Abstract

raj is experimenting with personal swarms of agents. He wants persistent project contexts, direct communication between agents, and clear control over work across machines. He is moving toward Autolith after trying a mixed set of agent systems.

Local agents already communicate and keep separate contexts. The proposed cross-machine system still needs trials. Its purpose is to support a personal computer science laboratory, with reproducible experiments, useful records, blogs, and eventually papers.

# Context

raj read David J. Moore's [A Taxonomy of Hierarchical Multi-Agent Systems: Design Patterns, Coordination Mechanisms, and Industrial Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.12683). Hierarchical multi-agent systems (HMAS) organize agents in layers. He is considering how to apply those ideas to personal work.

He tried Paperclip on a NixOS virtual private server, Hermes on a ThinkPad, and Autolith on a Mac. He now prefers Autolith heads across machines instead of this mixed setup. A head is the agent responsible for execution and resources on one machine.

Orch verified removal of the Paperclip and Hermes services from their active system configurations. The former services and endpoints are inactive. Data and rollback state were retained. The running and boot system profiles match on both machines, but reboot behavior was not tested.

The ThinkPad already had Autolith before this change. No replacement Autolith was installed on the virtual private server. The proposed organization of machine heads still needs implementation and tests. Removing the old services does not establish a working cluster.

# Separate contexts and one task owner

Persistent project agents keep the context for their own projects. They can communicate directly instead of requiring raj to repeat each report. Persistence means that an agent can resume its work. It does not require continuous inference.

Orch is the coordinating agent. It handles priorities across projects and requests for raj's attention. Machine heads manage local execution and resource conflicts. Project agents retain domain knowledge. One agent must own each task, even when other agents contribute.

raj is considering a shallow hierarchy. For example, Orch could also act as the Mac head at first. Adding machines should not require adding layers of coordination to every small task.

The current local workflow already includes separate project contexts and direct agent messages. Extending that workflow across machines needs separate transport, recovery, and permission checks. Local success does not prove remote readiness.

# Match the method to the work

Use direct tools for small, exact tasks. A command, file read, or calculation often needs no additional agent.

For independent work, use low-effort workers for clear, bounded tasks with explicit checks. Use medium-effort workers for implementation, debugging, unclear scope, or failed checks. Keep the main coordinator at medium effort unless raj chooses otherwise.

The reason is practical: delegation adds context transfer and review. Use it when independent work can improve the result or reduce elapsed time. More agents do not, by themselves, produce better research. More machines also do not multiply a shared provider quota.

Native Lisp peer discovery gives local agents structured session information. They can resolve a current peer without parsing a terminal status report. This identifies a local destination. It does not establish remote discovery or grant permission to act.

Shared files also do not prove shared runtime state. Two agents can read the same configuration while running different loaded definitions. Changes need an appropriate reload and a check of the active state.

# Make work resumable across machines

The proposed system needs a record for each task. That record should identify the objective, owner, machine, workspace, input revisions, permitted actions, budget, output location, and completion check.

Keep task identity separate from a running process. After a restart, an agent should recover its commitments and next permitted step. It should inspect existing jobs before starting replacements. An inactive agent context should use no inference budget.

Delivery, acceptance, execution, and verified completion are different states. A sent message is not proof that work finished. Keep results until the receiving agent acknowledges them.

Disconnects make retries difficult. If a reply is missing, inspect the actual state before repeating an action with side effects. Identify duplicate requests and bound the number of retries. For cancellation, check that the underlying jobs and child agents stopped.

These are requirements for the cross-machine design. They are not claims that remote recovery and cancellation have passed tests.

# Evaluate research, not agent activity

The long-term goal is a personal computer science laboratory. The cluster is one application within it. More messages or completed subtasks are weak evidence of research progress.

For an investigation, retain the question, code and input versions, environment, configuration, measurements, and uncertainty. Preserve negative results. Separate exploration from reproduction and review. A model's claim is not a measurement.

A useful first remote trial would produce a read-only artifact that another agent can check independently. Later trials should cover disconnects, duplicate delivery, restart, and cancellation. An isolated write task needs its own permission. Complete a real investigation before expanding the system.

Research output should pass verification before it reaches the blog or a paper.

# Conclusion

raj has chosen a direction: persistent Autolith agents with separate project contexts, direct communication, and a shallow structure for coordination. The local workflow provides a starting point. The proposed cross-machine system still needs verified transport, bounded tasks, recovery tests, and a first reproducible investigation.

---
title: Blog Update [0]
date: 2026-10-03
---

Previously, the blog was only a collection of posts in a table.  

I've setup a pipeline to sort of visualize semantics now: 
- first generate embeddings based on a change hash (post + embedding model tag) i.e. recompute only for recent delta
- store those in sqlite
- compute principal components and build the map(an svg).


## Math

Each post's title and visible Markdown text are split into non-overlapping chunks of at most 512 whitespace-delimited words and 2,048 model tokens (including special tokens), without truncation. The pinned [gte-modernbert-base](https://huggingface.co/Alibaba-NLP/gte-modernbert-base) model and its own pooling produce a 768-dimensional vector $e_{ic}$ for chunk $c$ of post $i$.

Normalize each chunk, average by its actual input-token count $t_{ic}$, then normalize the post:

$$
u_{ic} = \frac{e_{ic}}{\lVert e_{ic}\rVert_2},
\qquad m_i = \frac{\sum_c t_{ic}u_{ic}}{\sum_c t_{ic}},
\qquad v_i = \frac{m_i}{\lVert m_i\rVert_2}.
$$

Token weighting prevents a short final chunk from counting as much as a full chunk. One vector per post necessarily compresses its mixture of topics. Unit normalization relates Euclidean distance to cosine similarity:

$$
\lVert v_i-v_j\rVert_2^2 = 2(1-v_i^\top v_j).
$$

For $n\ge1$ posts, stack $v_i^\top$ as rows of $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times768}$, ordered by slug. Store vectors as float32; compute centered PCA in float64, subtracting the first row before the mean to preserve small differences:

$$
\mu = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i v_i,
\qquad C = X-\mathbf{1}\mu^\top,
\qquad C = U\Sigma V^\top.
$$

Use exact reduced SVD, with no per-dimension standardization or whitening. For $k=\min(2,n-1)$, the map coordinates are $Y=C V_k=U_k\Sigma_k$; missing coordinates are zero. Fix each component's sign so its largest-magnitude loading is positive. Use the same display scale on both axes.

The retained-variance fraction is:

$$
R = \frac{\sum_{r=1}^{k}\sigma_r^2}{\sum_r\sigma_r^2}.
$$

The heading displays $100R$ rounded to a whole percent. Three centered vectors span at most two dimensions, so two components retain all their variance. This measures projection fidelity, not semantic accuracy; with more posts, 2D distances can lose information. With no variation, the ratio is undefined and points coincide; an empty archive has no points. Refit PCA on each build, so positions can change.

## Usage Flow

1. Create a post with `./write.sh "Title"` and edit its Markdown in `meditations/`.
2. When ready, run `.venv-embed/bin/python scripts/embed.py`. SHA-256 keys cover the prepared title/body and complete pinned embedding specification. Only missing/changed vectors require inference; model/policy changes invalidate the archive. Date corrections, unchanged-content renames, and deletions synchronize without inference. Metadata and vectors are committed atomically to `blog.sqlite`.
3. Optionally preview: `.venv-embed/bin/python scripts/publish.py` builds `site/`; `.venv-embed/bin/python -m http.server 8765 --directory site` serves it locally.
4. Run `./publish.sh` on `master`: it checks freshness, then stages, commits, and pushes the posts and working database. Styling-only changes need no embedding update.
5. GitHub CI installs only publishing dependencies, checks committed embedding freshness, runs regressions, refits PCA, and builds HTML/SVG plus a fresh public SQLite snapshot. It uploads `site/` and deploys GitHub Pages to `yetanotherraj.com`. CI never runs embedding inference; stale state blocks deployment. Pull requests validate/build but do not deploy.

The most different sort of happiest (I don't like using that word but here we are) I've been in my life has been when I'm thinking about hard problems - haven't quite invested much into those lately and that's taken a toll on my cognitive health.  

This site as it stands right now serves as a collection of my laboratory notes. There's more I slowly plan on integrating over time but I'm going to be deliberate about it.  

I've ditched thinking through the fixed pipeline of pushing markdown through static site generators and instead am experimenting what all i could do in decoupled build stages - thinking more natively in the form higher order abstractions like data and transformations, where do i house / run each of them..  

This being my fourth or fifth personal cyber space over the span of 7+ years, have deliberately let go of all the rules. All previous moves were from the perspective of getting into a formulaic setup - this time, feels like slowly furnishing up a large empty warehouse - the initial days would be .., well .., a little empty, but I should pretty quickly converge on my own style.  

I plan on being a more mathematically inclined individual in this phase of my life - applied pragmatic mathematics is the primary higher order field that will influence the ideas that i have in the foreseeable future. So this is more of a think-out-loud in terms of what all i'd like in my personal research lab.  

I'm also a linguistics person and there was a time in one my past spaces where i used to maintain my own dictionary around words i coined to succinctly represent concepts that took more space. Thinking of bringing back a flavour of that in here.  

Computational epistemology is another domain that I'm building up cognitive senses for..  

There's a bunch more and i don't let the inter-domain boundaries wall me off from jumping those pseudo fences - i'll bring them out one by one over a bunch of future meditations..  

I do miss being ambitious for the sake of itself - going to chase that high again.

My first intentional knowledge management effort was prompted by the book circa 2019 - "how to take smart notes" by Ahrens Sönke - introducing the Zettelkasten.  

that was the first sentence that i wrote down and then i was going to present my past with knowledge graphs and how they aren't useful anymore.  

came up with a brief dump as follows(part of my writing process):

```
---

knowledge mangamenet 

notebooks before - emergent structure around notes - what helps , what doesn't

knowledge graphs

obsidian , couple of org roam ones, extensions for maintaining multiple roam vaults

why i gave up on emacs is a story for another day

not of much use - but of some use - pruning was important

LLMs into the mix -  2022

epistemology

## questions

what's useful?

 - connections? - graph - epistemological cartography
 - to be able to update them and make use of them
 - what makes a knowledge graph useful ? - that is the important question
 - what do you do of that knowledge? - when do you really start building knowledge graphs well
```

that was not supposed to be seen by you but i rally wanted to convey how i'm going about this well.  

i maintain a bunch of journals in a handy tmux, nvim popup and this is what i wrote while at this: 


```

 - good time to start doing this - NeSy wise - need to be able to get started with 
 - writing well and to learn feels too grainy on the brain right now - for too long, i've written like a hobo - time to return to my intellectual and rigorous roots
 - i'm just staring at a blank screen - that is kinda hard on my brain
 - alright - i guess it's time to start going on with the destructivist and creativist alternating approach when it comes to writing things down
 - start with a larger dump, cut down and orient and structure and the let the underlying message emerge from the process
 - don't focus on the small stuff first
 - emacs was good - having structure around how i work was good - now that i've worked without it for a while - need to start building my operational muscles again , this time being very deliberate around what i do and what i don't - infinite extensibility is not ideal - i did expose the internals well and would have been a right choice to stay in given the way software engineering in itself hadn't changed so much but now, the terminal is the way to go about this
 - what it means to use a computer in the present day has changed dramatically - the CLI never goes out of fashion i bet - it will probably always remain the most powerful layer of controlling and interacting with a computer i bet
 - the rest will all be layers that build on this one
 - why i gave up on emacs - what software engineering meant changed - spending all of the time in emacs is not a thing anymore - collaboration demands markdown and other tooling - before, when learning solo - i bet that was all fine and all but now, not anymore , need to start thinking about doing things more efficiently
 - tmux and neovim are the native drivers for everything now - honestly - it was lisp that made me go out there - now i don't really care about lisp as much so that is a thing - i would have stayed in tmux and vim if it wasn't for tmux out there - i did learn a lot though
 - as a consultant - domain knowledge when getting on a project needs to be ramped up on quickly - today, i'm going to spend a day sharpening the axe
 - will write on technical things henceforth - along the lines of writing to learn by William Zinsser
 - along the lines of writing to think is what i'll do - teaching and explaining a particular small concept would be nice
 - alright, i need to start being practical about how i do things henceforth - not single one off blog posts of whatever but more larger pieces of content
 - on charting an idea
```

My intent around these meditations is to "write to think" (realized during that journal entry) - that involves being a little more transparent and honest around what my brain is really upto when i'm thinking of a particular thing  

i don't care about punctuation or grammar or spelling well as much when i think - i understand why i do care about it so muc hwhen i publish  

writing for the sake of publishing feels off lately - why do i have to publish in a curated and polished manner - that is not really what i'm going for these days  

anyway don't like reading extremely curated stuff adn would just prefer the idea being conveyed as efficiently and rigorously as possible when i do to try that  

in the middle of this all , realized that i'm not this person to force myself to write like 1000 words a day and rack my brain around if a sentence sounds right?  

i'd rather iterate upon a 1000 essays, run higher order tooling and processing on those (LLM assisted summaries, visualize embeddings, note patterns, etc) to let the ideas emerge , instead of trying to force a conveyance in that one essay.  

bear with me while i figure out how does one write to think  

i shall get back to the idea of how do i really want to approach knowledge and meta-knowledge and my incentives around it ove rtime - that is somethign that deserves more than an essay and a lot more honesty  

i did go and read a wikipedia page on epistemology while going through this and realized that i would rather build my understanding empirically rather than retrofit my thought/thinking into predefined buckets/labels  

i'll be spending some more time evolving this process and being a whole lot emore honest aroudn how i like to analyse myt approach to maitnaing my ideas, in a compute assisted manner  

this might look ugly at first, but i do expect to converge to something useful soon before i actually get down to something better than i've done before - giving up a local optima in hopes of a global optima that's more natural to me down teh line  

i planned on being complete in this unit of conveyance (an essay) but i don't really have a definite answer as to why should i not just let this play out over time

title: programming
date: 2026-09-29

i liked using emacs and thinking in lisp for a long time. i gave those up a while ago. One doesn't really give up thinking in lisp - i mean i stopped trying to look at everything as s-expressions even though i could.   

Deromanticizing is the word i use around this recent effort/phase - i've been at it for around 2 months and i'm not enjoying working at all. i used to like the feel of over-caffeinating and titrating L-theanine, loading some tunes and just bashing away on my keyboard.  

i'm not really taking that too well - i miss loving programming - even ditched the whole bit-mage angle around exploring all of computer science and started exploring some hobbies outside the screen (stone carving/sculpting, motorcycles, etc).  

i still miss the feeling - couldn't really pin down the whole deromanticized take on things - don't think it extrapolates well for my mental health..  

i'm fairly young into my career still - it's just been 4 years so far of being a software engineer professionally and it feels like i've spent a bunch of epochs in terms of the way i think of it.  

it doesn't excite me anymore as much as it used to before - i can get more done and i know more than before and i'm better than before but i'm losing the joy around it - the joy to study more and know more.  

it all started with agentic engineering/programming not needing being crafty with your fingers anymore - you type and wait for longer and longer durations now - before, thinking and typing went along well. Now, not so much.  

LLMs ofcourse play a part but they aren't the core reason behind this overall emotional recession around the domain.  

i'm into the whole super user oriented HCI aspect (Human computer interaction) and like to share a certain awareness with the computer when i'm working with it.  

i tried filling in the vacuum of that with other kinds of intellectual hobbies - getting into math being the primary one - but that is engagement along some other cognitive dimension and i still feel a lack.  

i'm planning a revival though - writing like this, like i used to when i did my university days, not quite prioritizing polish and just logging, is the first step i'm taking towards it.  

i do like computer science, and do plan on spending a life with it but just happen to have hit a speed bump is my take..

i've ditched evalengizing emacs and lisp for i previously thought others would benefit knowing about that way of interacting with a computer; given LLMs though - that doesn't seem as necessary for them.  

i'll still continue to anticipate enjoying a lisp again - might start hand writing some soon again.  

it was a carrier for many of the more sophisticated abstractions i explored; since the drop, that has habit and the will to do so has deteriorated quite a lot.  

Don't quite know how i revive it though - simply have a strong intent to do so right now, the pragmatic question around - is it even worth it right now always comes back  

i am getting back into neovim and the whole unix way of doing things though. Before the 6 years with emacs, i spend 18 months in vim and the CLI and those were fun times too.

---
title: Project Outlines
date: 2026-10-01
---

Studying feels good - be that following a structured curriculum or unstructured exploration without any intent.  

The way one should be studying, given the times, is the subject of my meditations, fairly often now.  

Acquaintances lie across a spectrum:  some would power through corpora e2e, while some leverage LLMs to produce artifacts and wouldn't bat an eye over the raw docs.  

A bit of both, based on my mood in the moment, is what I do..  

Retrospecting, my studying bouts exhibit a few repeating patterns.  

Understanding all the domain specific terms independent of the text is what i do first. This might look like working in an outline - i picked this habit up from all the years spent in emacs and org mode. A tree data structure to represent concepts and recursing to the leaf nodes (constituent sub-concepts) that i comprehend is the first step i take towards breaking down a larger problem. I make sure i understand the tree from the bottom up if i have enough time (when this is a leisurely studying bout). When dealing with deadlines, compromises around being okay with just knowing the higher level "whats" around a node need to be made. This might lead to some back and forth when i hit a wall during a task, and i have to invest some more in the depth of a particular subtree.  

Next is a context-aware pass of the tree as a whole. That is, not just understanding the nodes independently but enriching what they mean given the other nodes in the tree.  

I build and maintain this concept tree (could be a markdown or an org file). I could get answers from the raw (not much really stays unparsed by an LLM these days, I believe, though) doc or through intent focused artifacts (generated with an intent in mind).  

Given this initial hierarchical outline (concept tree), given varying intent, i'll fork it off and iterate.  

This is one of the ways I like to approach a structured task.  

Unstructured exploration around a domain as a whole, when i don't have a strong seeding intent, would be treated separately in a future post.

Previously, the blog was only a collection of posts in a table.  

I've setup a pipeline to sort of visualize semantics now: 
- first generate embeddings based on a change hash (post + embedding model tag) i.e. recompute only for recent delta
- store those in sqlite
- compute principal components and build the map(an svg).


## Math

Each post's title and visible Markdown text are split into non-overlapping chunks of at most 512 whitespace-delimited words and 2,048 model tokens (including special tokens), without truncation. The pinned [gte-modernbert-base](https://huggingface.co/Alibaba-NLP/gte-modernbert-base) model and its own pooling produce a 768-dimensional vector $e_{ic}$ for chunk $c$ of post $i$.

Normalize each chunk, average by its actual input-token count $t_{ic}$, then normalize the post:

$$
u_{ic} = \frac{e_{ic}}{\lVert e_{ic}\rVert_2},
\qquad m_i = \frac{\sum_c t_{ic}u_{ic}}{\sum_c t_{ic}},
\qquad v_i = \frac{m_i}{\lVert m_i\rVert_2}.
$$

Token weighting prevents a short final chunk from counting as much as a full chunk. One vector per post necessarily compresses its mixture of topics. Unit normalization relates Euclidean distance to cosine similarity:

$$
\lVert v_i-v_j\rVert_2^2 = 2(1-v_i^\top v_j).
$$

For $n\ge1$ posts, stack $v_i^\top$ as rows of $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times768}$, ordered by slug. Store vectors as float32; compute centered PCA in float64, subtracting the first row before the mean to preserve small differences:

$$
\mu = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i v_i,
\qquad C = X-\mathbf{1}\mu^\top,
\qquad C = U\Sigma V^\top.
$$

Use exact reduced SVD, with no per-dimension standardization or whitening. For $k=\min(2,n-1)$, the map coordinates are $Y=C V_k=U_k\Sigma_k$; missing coordinates are zero. Fix each component's sign so its largest-magnitude loading is positive. Use the same display scale on both axes.

The retained-variance fraction is:

$$
R = \frac{\sum_{r=1}^{k}\sigma_r^2}{\sum_r\sigma_r^2}.
$$

The heading displays $100R$ rounded to a whole percent. Three centered vectors span at most two dimensions, so two components retain all their variance. This measures projection fidelity, not semantic accuracy; with more posts, 2D distances can lose information. With no variation, the ratio is undefined and points coincide; an empty archive has no points. Refit PCA on each build, so positions can change.

## Usage Flow

1. Create a post with `./write.sh "Title"` and edit its Markdown in `meditations/`.
2. When ready, run `.venv-embed/bin/python scripts/embed.py`. SHA-256 keys cover the prepared title/body and complete pinned embedding specification. Only missing/changed vectors require inference; model/policy changes invalidate the archive. Date corrections, unchanged-content renames, and deletions synchronize without inference. Metadata and vectors are committed atomically to `blog.sqlite`.
3. Optionally preview: `.venv-embed/bin/python scripts/publish.py` builds `site/`; `.venv-embed/bin/python -m http.server 8765 --directory site` serves it locally.
4. Run `./publish.sh` on `master`: it checks freshness, then stages, commits, and pushes the posts and working database. Styling-only changes need no embedding update.
5. GitHub CI installs only publishing dependencies, checks committed embedding freshness, runs regressions, refits PCA, and builds HTML/SVG plus a fresh public SQLite snapshot. It uploads `site/` and deploys GitHub Pages to `yetanotherraj.com`. CI never runs embedding inference; stale state blocks deployment. Pull requests validate/build but do not deploy.

# Abstract

raj is experimenting with personal swarms of agents. He wants persistent project contexts, direct communication between agents, and clear control over work across machines. He is moving toward Autolith after trying a mixed set of agent systems.

Local agents already communicate and keep separate contexts. The proposed cross-machine system still needs trials. Its purpose is to support a personal computer science laboratory, with reproducible experiments, useful records, blogs, and eventually papers.

# Context

raj read David J. Moore's [A Taxonomy of Hierarchical Multi-Agent Systems: Design Patterns, Coordination Mechanisms, and Industrial Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.12683). Hierarchical multi-agent systems (HMAS) organize agents in layers. He is considering how to apply those ideas to personal work.

He tried Paperclip on a NixOS virtual private server, Hermes on a ThinkPad, and Autolith on a Mac. He now prefers Autolith heads across machines instead of this mixed setup. A head is the agent responsible for execution and resources on one machine.

Orch verified removal of the Paperclip and Hermes services from their active system configurations. The former services and endpoints are inactive. Data and rollback state were retained. The running and boot system profiles match on both machines, but reboot behavior was not tested.

The ThinkPad already had Autolith before this change. No replacement Autolith was installed on the virtual private server. The proposed organization of machine heads still needs implementation and tests. Removing the old services does not establish a working cluster.

# Separate contexts and one task owner

Persistent project agents keep the context for their own projects. They can communicate directly instead of requiring raj to repeat each report. Persistence means that an agent can resume its work. It does not require continuous inference.

Orch is the coordinating agent. It handles priorities across projects and requests for raj's attention. Machine heads manage local execution and resource conflicts. Project agents retain domain knowledge. One agent must own each task, even when other agents contribute.

raj is considering a shallow hierarchy. For example, Orch could also act as the Mac head at first. Adding machines should not require adding layers of coordination to every small task.

The current local workflow already includes separate project contexts and direct agent messages. Extending that workflow across machines needs separate transport, recovery, and permission checks. Local success does not prove remote readiness.

# Match the method to the work

Use direct tools for small, exact tasks. A command, file read, or calculation often needs no additional agent.

For independent work, use low-effort workers for clear, bounded tasks with explicit checks. Use medium-effort workers for implementation, debugging, unclear scope, or failed checks. Keep the main coordinator at medium effort unless raj chooses otherwise.

The reason is practical: delegation adds context transfer and review. Use it when independent work can improve the result or reduce elapsed time. More agents do not, by themselves, produce better research. More machines also do not multiply a shared provider quota.

Native Lisp peer discovery gives local agents structured session information. They can resolve a current peer without parsing a terminal status report. This identifies a local destination. It does not establish remote discovery or grant permission to act.

Shared files also do not prove shared runtime state. Two agents can read the same configuration while running different loaded definitions. Changes need an appropriate reload and a check of the active state.

# Make work resumable across machines

The proposed system needs a record for each task. That record should identify the objective, owner, machine, workspace, input revisions, permitted actions, budget, output location, and completion check.

Keep task identity separate from a running process. After a restart, an agent should recover its commitments and next permitted step. It should inspect existing jobs before starting replacements. An inactive agent context should use no inference budget.

Delivery, acceptance, execution, and verified completion are different states. A sent message is not proof that work finished. Keep results until the receiving agent acknowledges them.

Disconnects make retries difficult. If a reply is missing, inspect the actual state before repeating an action with side effects. Identify duplicate requests and bound the number of retries. For cancellation, check that the underlying jobs and child agents stopped.

These are requirements for the cross-machine design. They are not claims that remote recovery and cancellation have passed tests.

# Evaluate research, not agent activity

The long-term goal is a personal computer science laboratory. The cluster is one application within it. More messages or completed subtasks are weak evidence of research progress.

For an investigation, retain the question, code and input versions, environment, configuration, measurements, and uncertainty. Preserve negative results. Separate exploration from reproduction and review. A model's claim is not a measurement.

A useful first remote trial would produce a read-only artifact that another agent can check independently. Later trials should cover disconnects, duplicate delivery, restart, and cancellation. An isolated write task needs its own permission. Complete a real investigation before expanding the system.

Research output should pass verification before it reaches the blog or a paper.

# Conclusion

raj has chosen a direction: persistent Autolith agents with separate project contexts, direct communication, and a shallow structure for coordination. The local workflow provides a starting point. The proposed cross-machine system still needs verified transport, bounded tasks, recovery tests, and a first reproducible investigation.

Previously, the blog was only a collection of posts in a table.  

I've setup a pipeline to sort of visualize semantics now: 
- first generate embeddings based on a change hash (post + embedding model tag) i.e. recompute only for recent delta
- store those in sqlite
- compute principal components and build the map(an svg).


## Math

Each post's title and visible Markdown text are split into non-overlapping chunks of at most 512 whitespace-delimited words and 2,048 model tokens (including special tokens), without truncation. The pinned [gte-modernbert-base](https://huggingface.co/Alibaba-NLP/gte-modernbert-base) model and its own pooling produce a 768-dimensional vector $e_{ic}$ for chunk $c$ of post $i$.

Normalize each chunk, average by its actual input-token count $t_{ic}$, then normalize the post:

$$
u_{ic} = \frac{e_{ic}}{\lVert e_{ic}\rVert_2},
\qquad m_i = \frac{\sum_c t_{ic}u_{ic}}{\sum_c t_{ic}},
\qquad v_i = \frac{m_i}{\lVert m_i\rVert_2}.
$$

Token weighting prevents a short final chunk from counting as much as a full chunk. One vector per post necessarily compresses its mixture of topics. Unit normalization relates Euclidean distance to cosine similarity:

$$
\lVert v_i-v_j\rVert_2^2 = 2(1-v_i^\top v_j).
$$

For $n\ge1$ posts, stack $v_i^\top$ as rows of $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times768}$, ordered by slug. Store vectors as float32; compute centered PCA in float64, subtracting the first row before the mean to preserve small differences:

$$
\mu = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i v_i,
\qquad C = X-\mathbf{1}\mu^\top,
\qquad C = U\Sigma V^\top.
$$

Use exact reduced SVD, with no per-dimension standardization or whitening. For $k=\min(2,n-1)$, the map coordinates are $Y=C V_k=U_k\Sigma_k$; missing coordinates are zero. Fix each component's sign so its largest-magnitude loading is positive. Use the same display scale on both axes.

The retained-variance fraction is:

$$
R = \frac{\sum_{r=1}^{k}\sigma_r^2}{\sum_r\sigma_r^2}.
$$

The heading displays $100R$ rounded to a whole percent. Three centered vectors span at most two dimensions, so two components retain all their variance. This measures projection fidelity, not semantic accuracy; with more posts, 2D distances can lose information. With no variation, the ratio is undefined and points coincide; an empty archive has no points. Refit PCA on each build, so positions can change.

## Usage Flow

1. Create a post with `./write.sh "Title"` and edit its Markdown in `meditations/`.
2. When ready, run `.venv-embed/bin/python scripts/embed.py`. SHA-256 keys cover the prepared title/body and complete pinned embedding specification. Only missing/changed vectors require inference; model/policy changes invalidate the archive. Date corrections, unchanged-content renames, and deletions synchronize without inference. Metadata and vectors are committed atomically to `blog.sqlite`.
3. Optionally preview: `.venv-embed/bin/python scripts/publish.py` builds `site/`; `.venv-embed/bin/python -m http.server 8765 --directory site` serves it locally.
4. Run `./publish.sh` on `master`: it checks freshness, then stages, commits, and pushes the posts and working database. Styling-only changes need no embedding update.
5. GitHub CI installs only publishing dependencies, checks committed embedding freshness, runs regressions, refits PCA, and builds HTML/SVG plus a fresh public SQLite snapshot. It uploads `site/` and deploys GitHub Pages to `yetanotherraj.com`. CI never runs embedding inference; stale state blocks deployment. Pull requests validate/build but do not deploy.

---
title: Personal (Knowledge -> Epistemological) Management
date: 2026-09-25
---

My first intentional knowledge management effort was prompted by the book circa 2019 - "how to take smart notes" by Ahrens Sönke - introducing the Zettelkasten.  

that was the first sentence that i wrote down and then i was going to present my past with knowledge graphs and how they aren't useful anymore.  

came up with a brief dump as follows(part of my writing process):

```
---

knowledge mangamenet 

notebooks before - emergent structure around notes - what helps , what doesn't

knowledge graphs

obsidian , couple of org roam ones, extensions for maintaining multiple roam vaults

why i gave up on emacs is a story for another day

multiple wiki phases over that period of time - nuke the past ones
 - links in footnotes

not of much use - but of some use - pruning was important

LLMs into the mix -  2022

epistemology

## questions

what's useful?

 - connections? - graph - epistemological cartography
 - to be able to update them and make use of them
 - what makes a knowledge graph useful ? - that is the important question
 - what do you do of that knowledge? - when do you really start building knowledge graphs well
```

that was not supposed to be seen by you but i rally wanted to convey how i'm going about this well.  

i maintain a bunch of journals in a handy tmux, nvim popup and this is what i wrote while at this: 


```
 - as i onboard onto a new project - going to spend some time building the epistemology layer around the project so that i can iterate over time - it should be small and shouldn't change a lot over time
 - good time to start doing this - NeSy wise - need to be able to get started with 
 - writing well and to learn feels too grainy on the brain right now - for too long, i've written like a hobo - time to return to my intellectual and rigorous roots
 - i'm just staring at a blank screen - that is kinda hard on my brain
 - alright - i guess it's time to start going on with the destructivist and creativist alternating approach when it comes to writing things down
 - start with a larger dump, cut down and orient and structure and the let the underlying message emerge from the process
 - don't focus on the small stuff first
 - emacs was good - having structure around how i work was good - now that i've worked without it for a while - need to start building my operational muscles again , this time being very deliberate around what i do and what i don't - infinite extensibility is not ideal - i did expose the internals well and would have been a right choice to stay in given the way software engineering in itself hadn't changed so much but now, the terminal is the way to go about this
 - what it means to use a computer in the present day has changed dramatically - the CLI never goes out of fashion i bet - it will probably always remain the most powerful layer of controlling and interacting with a computer i bet
 - the rest will all be layers that build on this one
 - why i gave up on emacs - what software engineering meant changed - spending all of the time in emacs is not a thing anymore - collaboration demands markdown and other tooling - before, when learning solo - i bet that was all fine and all but now, not anymore , need to start thinking about doing things more efficiently
 - tmux and neovim are the native drivers for everything now - honestly - it was lisp that made me go out there - now i don't really care about lisp as much so that is a thing - i would have stayed in tmux and vim if it wasn't for tmux out there - i did learn a lot though
 - as a consultant - domain knowledge when getting on a project needs to be ramped up on quickly - today, i'm going to spend a day sharpening the axe
 - will write on technical things henceforth - along the lines of writing to learn by William Zinsser
 - along the lines of writing to think is what i'll do - teaching and explaining a particular small concept would be nice
 - alright, i need to start being practical about how i do things henceforth - not single one off blog posts of whatever but more larger pieces of content
 - on charting an idea
```

writing and curating is quite non-linear and involves a bunch of recursive refinement around ideas. My intent around these meditations is to "write to think" (realized during that journal entry) - that involves being a little more transparent and honest around what my brain is really upto when i'm thinking of a particular thing  

i don't care about punctuation or grammar or spelling well as much when i think - i understand why i do care about it so muc hwhen i publish  

writing for the sake of publishing feels off lately - why do i have to publish in a curated and polished manner - that is not really what i'm going for these days  

anyway don't like reading extremely curated stuff adn would just prefer the idea being conveyed as efficiently and rigorously as possible when i do to try that  

in the middle of this all , realized that i'm not this person to force myself to write like 1000 words a day and rack my brain around if a sentence sounds right?  

i'd rather iterate upon a 1000 essays, run higher order tooling and processing on those (LLM assisted summaries, visualize embeddings, note patterns, etc) to let the ideas emerge , instead of trying to force a conveyance in that one essay.  

bear with me while i figure out how does one write to think  

i shall get back to the idea of how do i really want to approach knowledge and meta-knowledge and my incentives around it ove rtime - that is somethign that deserves more than an essay and a lot more honesty  

i did go and read a wikipedia page on epistemology while going through this and realized that i would rather build my understanding empirically rather than retrofit my thought/thinking into predefined buckets/labels  

i'll be spending some more time evolving this process and being a whole lot emore honest aroudn how i like to analyse myt approach to maitnaing my ideas, in a compute assisted manner  

this might look ugly at first, but i do expect to converge to something useful soon before i actually get down to something better than i've done before - giving up a local optima in hopes of a global optima that's more natural to me down teh line  

i planned on being complete in this unit of conveyance (an essay) but i don't really have a definite answer as to why should i not just let this play out over time  

alrgiht, should have a SaaS aroudn "writing to think" as well sometime soon

title: programming

i liked using emacs and thinking in lisp for a long time. i gave those up a while ago. One doesn't really give up thinking in lisp - i mean i stopped trying to look at everything as s-expressions even though i could.   

Deromanticizing is the word i use around this recent effort/phase - i've been at it for around 2 months and i'm not enjoying working at all. i used to like the feel of over-caffeinating and titrating L-theanine, loading some tunes and just bashing away on my keyboard.  

i'm not really taking that too well - i miss loving programming - even ditched the whole bit-mage angle around exploring all of computer science and started exploring some hobbies outside the screen (stone carving/sculpting, motorcycles, etc).  

i still miss the feeling - couldn't really pin down the whole deromanticized take on things - don't think it extrapolates well for my mental health..  

i'm fairly young into my career still - it's just been 4 years so far of being a software engineer professionally and it feels like i've spent a bunch of epochs in terms of the way i think of it.  

it doesn't excite me anymore as much as it used to before - i can get more done and i know more than before and i'm better than before but i'm losing the joy around it - the joy to study more and know more.  

it all started with agentic engineering/programming not needing being crafty with your fingers anymore - you type and wait for longer and longer durations now - before, thinking and typing went along well. Now, not so much.  

LLMs ofcourse play a part but they aren't the core reason behind this overall emotional recession around the domain.  

i'm into the whole super user oriented HCI aspect (Human computer interaction) and like to share a certain awareness with the computer when i'm working with it.  

i tried filling in the vacuum of that with other kinds of intellectual hobbies - getting into math being the primary one - but that is engagement along some other cognitive dimension and i still feel a lack.  

i'm planning a revival though - writing like this, like i used to when i did my university days, not quite prioritizing polish and just logging, is the first step i'm taking towards it.  

i do like computer science, and do plan on spending a life with it but just happen to have hit a speed bump is my take..

i've ditched evalengizing emacs and lisp for i previously thought others would benefit knowing about that way of interacting with a computer; given LLMs though - that doesn't seem as necessary for them.  

i'll still continue to anticipate enjoying a lisp again - might start hand writing some soon again.  

it was a carrier for many of the more sophisticated abstractions i explored; since the drop, that has habit and the will to do so has deteriorated quite a lot.  

Don't quite know how i revive it though - simply have a strong intent to do so right now, the pragmatic question around - is it even worth it right now always comes back  

i am getting back into neovim and the whole unix way of doing things though. Before the 6 years with emacs, i spend 18 months in vim and the CLI and those were fun times too.

Studying feels good - be that following a structured curriculum or unstructured exploration without any intent.  

The way one should be studying, given the times, is the subject of my meditations, fairly often now.

A bit of both, based on my mood in the moment, is what I do..  

Retrospecting, my studying bouts exhibit a few repeating patterns.  

Understanding all the domain specific terms independent of the text is what i do first. This might look like working in an outline - i picked this habit up from all the years spent in emacs and org mode. A tree data structure to represent concepts and recursing to the leaf nodes (constituent sub-concepts) that i comprehend is the first step i take towards breaking down a larger problem. I make sure i understand the tree from the bottom up if i have enough time (when this is a leisurely studying bout). When dealing with deadlines, compromises around being okay with just knowing the higher level "whats" around a node need to be made. This might lead to some back and forth when i hit a wall during a task, and i have to invest some more in the depth of a particular subtree.  

Next is a context-aware pass of the tree as a whole. That is, not just understanding the nodes independently but enriching what they mean given the other nodes in the tree.  

I build and maintain this concept tree (could be a markdown or an org file). I could get answers from the raw (not much really stays unparsed by an LLM these days, I believe, though) doc or through intent focused artifacts (generated with an intent in mind).  

Given this initial hierarchical outline (concept tree), given varying intent, i'll fork it off and iterate.  

This is one of the ways I like to approach a structured task.  

Unstructured exploration around a domain as a whole, when i don't have a strong seeding intent, would be treated separately in a future post.

title: Blog Update [0]
date: 2026-10-03
---

Previously, the blog was only a collection of posts in a table.  

I've setup a pipeline to sort of visualize semantics now: 
- first generate embeddings based on a change hash (post + embedding model tag) i.e. recompute only for recent delta
- store those in sqlite
- compute principal components and build the map(an svg).


## Math

Each post's title and visible Markdown text are split into non-overlapping chunks of at most 512 whitespace-delimited words and 2,048 model tokens (including special tokens), without truncation. The pinned [gte-modernbert-base](https://huggingface.co/Alibaba-NLP/gte-modernbert-base) model and its own pooling produce a 768-dimensional vector $e_{ic}$ for chunk $c$ of post $i$.

Normalize each chunk, average by its actual input-token count $t_{ic}$, then normalize the post:

$$
u_{ic} = \frac{e_{ic}}{\lVert e_{ic}\rVert_2},
\qquad m_i = \frac{\sum_c t_{ic}u_{ic}}{\sum_c t_{ic}},
\qquad v_i = \frac{m_i}{\lVert m_i\rVert_2}.
$$

Token weighting prevents a short final chunk from counting as much as a full chunk. One vector per post necessarily compresses its mixture of topics. Unit normalization relates Euclidean distance to cosine similarity:

$$
\lVert v_i-v_j\rVert_2^2 = 2(1-v_i^\top v_j).
$$

For $n\ge1$ posts, stack $v_i^\top$ as rows of $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times768}$, ordered by slug. Store vectors as float32; compute centered PCA in float64, subtracting the first row before the mean to preserve small differences:

$$
\mu = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i v_i,
\qquad C = X-\mathbf{1}\mu^\top,
\qquad C = U\Sigma V^\top.
$$

Use exact reduced SVD, with no per-dimension standardization or whitening. For $k=\min(2,n-1)$, the map coordinates are $Y=C V_k=U_k\Sigma_k$; missing coordinates are zero. Fix each component's sign so its largest-magnitude loading is positive. Use the same display scale on both axes.

The retained-variance fraction is:

$$
R = \frac{\sum_{r=1}^{k}\sigma_r^2}{\sum_r\sigma_r^2}.
$$

The heading displays $100R$ rounded to a whole percent. Three centered vectors span at most two dimensions, so two components retain all their variance. This measures projection fidelity, not semantic accuracy; with more posts, 2D distances can lose information. With no variation, the ratio is undefined and points coincide; an empty archive has no points. Refit PCA on each build, so positions can change.

## Usage Flow

1. Create a post with `./write.sh "Title"` and edit its Markdown in `meditations/`.
2. When ready, run `.venv-embed/bin/python scripts/embed.py`. SHA-256 keys cover the prepared title/body and complete pinned embedding specification. Only missing/changed vectors require inference; model/policy changes invalidate the archive. Date corrections, unchanged-content renames, and deletions synchronize without inference. Metadata and vectors are committed atomically to `blog.sqlite`.
3. Optionally preview: `.venv-embed/bin/python scripts/publish.py` builds `site/`; `.venv-embed/bin/python -m http.server 8765 --directory site` serves it locally.
4. Run `./publish.sh` on `master`: it checks freshness, then stages, commits, and pushes the posts and working database. Styling-only changes need no embedding update.
5. GitHub CI installs only publishing dependencies, checks committed embedding freshness, runs regressions, refits PCA, and builds HTML/SVG plus a fresh public SQLite snapshot. It uploads `site/` and deploys GitHub Pages to `yetanotherraj.com`. CI never runs embedding inference; stale state blocks deployment. Pull requests validate/build but do not deploy.

# Abstract

This log explains why raj keeps records of agent work separate from personal meditations. Both collections use one archive.

# Context

raj wants a record of work that agents do at raj's request. The blog already holds raj's personal writing. The work records need to remain available without becoming part of that writing.

# Different authors

raj writes meditations. Agents write logs when raj asks for a record. The separate collections make this difference clear.

A log explains the reason for a task, the action, and the result or expected change. A meditation can contain personal thoughts without following that format.

# One place to find entries

Separate collections do not need separate search systems. The same index, search, and map include both collections. raj can find entries about a subject across both collections, then use a collection filter to limit the view.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  accTitle: Separate authors, one archive
  accDescr: raj writes meditations. Agents write logs at raj's request. Both collections enter the shared archive.
  R[raj] --> M[Meditations]
  R -->|Requests a record| A[Agents]
  A --> L[Logs]
  M --> S[Shared archive]
  L --> S
```

# Clear source labels

The index uses `mx` codes for meditations and `lx` codes for logs. Each collection has its own number sequence. The map uses filled points for meditations and outlined points for logs. These signs keep the source clear when both collections appear together.

# Review before publication

Each log has only a title and date before the text. Links can connect a log to earlier meditations and blogs.

raj can review and revise a local draft before asking for a commit. A revision does not approve a commit. A commit does not approve publication.

# Conclusion

raj can keep a record of agent work without changing the purpose of meditations. Both remain easy to find in one archive.
